36: Even though, etc., it is a mitzvah of the Chachamim, etc. — See the responsum of the Maharshal siman 35, who ruled that even where they accepted him upon themselves and he is a mumcheh, it is forbidden for him to judge alone, and he brought proofs; and in the responsa Sheiris Yosef siman 17 he disagreed with him and rejected his proofs, and so ruled the Bach. And in truth, the incident of the Yerushalmi that is brought in the long Mordechai and in the Baal HaIttur daf 51 amud beis is a refutation of the Maharshal, for it states there explicitly that Rabbi Abahu would judge alone, and his students said to him, "but we learned, do not judge alone," and he answered them, "since they come of their own accord to be judged before me, it is as if they accepted me," etc. — see there; and so it is explained more in the Yerushalmi itself at the start of the first perek of Sanhedrin — see there. However, regarding the law nowadays, in this time when there is no mumcheh, it requires study, for one can say that Rabbi Abahu is different, since he was a mumcheh, and acceptance helps specifically with a mumcheh; and so it is proven in the Yerushalmi there, which establishes Rabbi Abahu's [explanation of] the Mishnah in Bechoros — "one who judged the din, etc., what is done is done and he pays from his own [pocket]" — as referring to where they said to him "behold you are accepted upon us as three, on condition that you judge us by Torah law," that he pays from his own [pocket] since he was presumptuous to judge Torah law, for we learned "do not judge alone," etc. — end of the Yerushalmi's words, and the Baal HaIttur brings it there. (And therefore the latter clause of the Mishnah in Bechoros teaches "and if he was a mumcheh for the beis din he is exempt from paying.") And one cannot say that there it is different, because they stipulated with him explicitly that he should judge Torah law, for the Rosh and Tur write below in siman 25 that a plain acceptance before one who is not a mumcheh is with the intent that he judge Torah law — see there. But with one who is not a mumcheh, one can say that he should not judge l'chatchilah; and so it is implied explicitly in the Rosh, perek Echad Dinei Mamonos, who wrote in this language: "since he undertook from the outset to judge and he is not a mumcheh, it is fitting that he pay from his own [pocket], and even though they accepted [him] upon themselves, nonetheless he should not have judged alone since he is not a mumcheh," end quote. And according to this, those who are accustomed to judge alone where [the parties] come of their own accord to be judged, or even where they accepted him, are not acting properly, since nowadays there is no mumcheh. And it is possible that those who are accustomed to judge alone, that is in matters that are common and simple, in which they are mumchim; or it is possible that this itself is the reason — that since nowadays there is no mumcheh, and there is none wise in judgment nowadays, as it states in the Yerushalmi (and the Sma"g brings it, siman 107, and the Tur below siman 12, that nowadays there is none wise enough in judgment to judge Torah law) — then when they accepted him plainly, presumably they accepted him both for [correct] judgment and for error, and it resembles what the Nimukei Yosef wrote at the start of the first perek of Sanhedrin in the name of "some say," that if they accepted upon themselves yoshvei keranos (unlearned commoners), their ruling is a [valid] ruling, and even if they erred they are not liable to pay, for they cannot say that they accepted them with the intent that they judge them Torah law, for they surely know that they do not know Torah law. However, this requires study, for all the poskim did not bring the Yerushalmi that nowadays there is none wise enough to judge Torah law; and it appears that even the Sma"g and the Tur who brought it, it is only regarding that one should do whatever is possible to make a compromise (peshara), and so it is implied explicitly from the fact that they brought it regarding making a peshara, and wrote "the judges must distance themselves with all their ability that they should not accept upon themselves to judge Torah law, for we learned in the Yerushalmi, etc." — which implies explicitly that it is specifically l'chatchilah that they must distance themselves in this; but certainly even nowadays they know how to judge Torah law in many dinim that are explicit in the Gemara and poskim. Therefore, certainly when [the parties] come from the outset to be judged before him and accepted him, presumably they accepted him with the intent to be judged by Torah law, as the poskim and the Rosh and Tur write below siman 25; and therefore one must be careful not to judge alone even where they accepted him, unless he explicitly states "I do not know how to judge you by Torah law," or it is a simple din and he is a mumcheh and accustomed in it, for in such a case there is a mumcheh even nowadays — analyze this.
